description:
FOUND s493 (Fable, 2026-09-20) by the ONE-LINER battery (perl1line.txt #28/#29: `perl -le 'print $n=()=<>'`), narrowed in ~/pcl-agent-scratch/s493/angles/oneliners/countof.pl (perl 5.40.3 vs main 5316d666):

    open my $fh, "<", $f; my $n = () = <$fh>;            perl 18   PCL 1
    open $fh, "<", $f;    my ($first, @rest) = <$fh>;    perl 17 in @rest   PCL 0
    print scalar(() = <$fh>);                            perl 18   PCL 1
    my @all = <$fh>;  my @all = (<$fh>);                 both right (control)
    my $m = () = "a,b,c" =~ /\w/g;  my $k = () = lst();  both right (control)

So readline is given SCALAR context when the list-assignment's LHS is not a plain array: the context of the RHS is being derived from the LHS SHAPE instead of from "this is a list assignment".  `my ($header, @rows) = <$fh>;` is the everyday CSV/report idiom, and it fails SILENTLY (no rows).  Suspect sibling of #2004 (scalar context leaking into list-operator arguments) -- check whether ONE mechanism decides both.
MEASURE FIRST: the emission of the three failing lines vs `my @all = <$fh>` (which p-readline context keyword each gets).  PROBE THE BREAKING CASE: `my ($line) = <$fh>;` is a LIST assignment too in perl (it reads ALL lines and keeps the first!) -- perl's answer, not intuition, is the bar; `my $line = <$fh>` stays scalar; `($a, $b) = (<$fh>, <$fh>)`; `<STDIN>` and `<>` spellings; `readline($fh)` function form; `glob`/`<*.c>` on the same LHS shapes.
Also seen there (edge, same probe): `my $s = () = split /,/, "a,b,c,d"` is 1 in perl (split's implicit LIMIT when assigning to an empty list) and 4 in PCL -- note it, do not chase it.
Guard: Pl/t rows beside #2004's.


=== DONE (s492b, 2026-09-21) ===
SHIPPED in commit "#2090: <FH> on the RHS of a LIST assignment is LIST context -- the
*p-in-list-assign-rhs* flag goes".

ONE MECHANISM WITH #2004?  No -- MEASURED, and that is the finding.  #2004 is the compiler's
argument-context annotation; this was a SECOND variable in the RUNTIME beside *wantarray*:
*p-in-list-assign-rhs*, which p-list-= bound T around its whole RHS and p-readline / p-glob
consulted, so every list assignment read exactly one record.

THE FLAG'S PREMISE WAS FALSE, probed against perl 5.40.3:
  * `while (my ($x) = <FH>)` iterates ONCE in perl -- the RHS is list context and the first read
    slurps the handle.  (So `my ($line) = <$fh>` reading every line and keeping the first IS perl.)
  * `while (($seen ? $dummy : $name) = <FILE>)` iterates once per line not because readline is
    special there but because A TERNARY IS NOT A LIST: `($s ? $d : $n) = @a` stores the COUNT, so
    that statement is a SCALAR assignment.  `B::Deparse -p` wraps exactly that one in `defined(...)`
    and leaves `(($x) = readline(FILE))` alone.
ExprToCL's `_sole_ternary_lvalue_id` arm has lowered the ternary shape as a scalar assignment since
long before now, so the flag had become dead weight that was still costing correctness.  The defvar,
its export, its binding in p-list-= , its binding in Parser.pm's `local(...) = LIST` path and its
two consumers are deleted; ir-inventory regenerated.

perl-tests/defins.t -- the file the flag was added for -- stays 27/27.
docs/p-list-readline-conflict.md keeps the analysis with a RESOLVED header saying which half of it
was wrong.  NORMATIVE: docs/ir-spec.md 4.1, second bullet.
GUARDS: Pl/t/readline-ternary-01.t gains a #2090 block (three positives, two negatives; rows 25-27
fail on a 5ce155cb extraction) and Pl/t/glob-01.t gains the list-assignment glob row.
NOTED, NOT CHASED (as the task said): `my $s = () = split /,/, "a,b,c,d"` is 1 in perl (split's
implicit LIMIT when assigning to an empty list) and 4 here.
subject: SILENT WRONG (everyday): `<$fh>` on the RHS of a LIST assignment whose LHS is `()` or `my ($first, @rest)` reads ONE line -- `my ($header, @rows) = <$fh>` leaves @rows EMPTY; `my $n = () = <$fh>` is 1
